Monthly deficits are always surpluses
Debt cannot be compared with flows
It lacks a meaningful stock-flow time basis
before.feedback: Stocks and flows can be related, but the period and interpretation must be specified; this ratio is not a growth rate.

after.q: At year-end a government owes $2,400 billion. During the final month its deficit was $20 billion. An analyst divides 2,400 by 20 and calls the result a 120 percent annual debt-growth rate. If the monthly deficit instead remained constant for a full future year, all deficits were borrowed, and no other debt adjustments occurred, what would the calculation establish?
options: The original quotient is a 120 percent growth rate; annualizing the deficit leaves that rate unchanged
The original quotient is 120 years of deficits; the stated future scenario implies 1 percent annual debt growth
The original quotient is a 10 percent growth rate; dividing it by 12 gives annual debt growth
The original quotient is 120 months of deficits; the stated future scenario implies 10 percent annual debt growth
after.feedback: A stock of $2,400 billion divided by a flow of $20 billion per month gives 120 months, not a percent growth rate. Under the explicit future assumption, twelve monthly deficits add $240 billion to debt; 240 / 2,400 = 10 percent. One observed month alone does not establish that future path.

before.q: A claim says all borrowing is harmful because it raises debt. What is the best economic response?
options: The assessment depends partly on what the borrowing finances
Borrowing has no costs under any circumstances
Any positive deficit proves that national saving has fallen to zero
Economic analysis alone determines the only acceptable philosophy of fiscal policy
before.feedback: Positive analysis identifies accounting effects and conditional tradeoffs without turning them into a universal normative verdict.

after.q: Two packages require the same additional borrowing, leave public saving equally lower, and face the same unchanged private-saving and investment-demand schedules. Package A finances productive public infrastructure; Package B finances transfers. What evidence is needed to decide whether A leaves more total productive capital than before the policy?
options: Whether the public-capital addition exceeds the private-capital formation displaced by the higher real rate
Whether A issues less debt than B, even though their additional borrowing is stated to be equal
Whether transfers count as current public-capital formation at the moment they are paid
Whether a decline in public saving is itself a one-for-one measure of lost private capital
after.feedback: Both packages create the same initial loanable-funds pressure under the stated schedules. A also adds public productive capital. Its net capital effect depends on that addition relative to displaced private capital formation; borrowing alone does not establish the sign. No project-valuation or AD-AS model is needed for this comparison.

before.q: A larger deficit reduces public saving. Which conclusion is justified without solving for the exact loanable-funds equilibrium?
options: The exact equilibrium real interest rate must fall by the deficit percentage
A loanable-funds graph must shift by a fixed distance
Greater government borrowing can put upward pressure on interest rates and downward pressure on private investment.
Foreign capital inflows necessarily equal the deficit
before.feedback: A larger deficit lowers public saving; in the loanable-funds model, this can reduce national saving and put upward pressure on the real interest rate and downward pressure on private investment, but the exact equilibrium change requires the full model.

after.q: A deficit reduces public saving at every real rate. A separate household incentive exactly offsets that reduction in planned private saving at every rate, while an investment tax credit also raises desired investment. In the closed-economy loanable-funds model, what can be concluded relative to the initial equilibrium?
options: The saving curve shifts left; the real rate rises and private investment must fall
Both curves are unchanged; exact private-saving offset also cancels the investment tax credit
The saving curve is unchanged; the real rate and equilibrium private investment rise
The saving curve shifts right; private investment rises but the real rate must fall
after.feedback: The public- and private-saving shifts cancel at every rate, leaving national-saving supply unchanged. The tax credit separately shifts investment demand right. With an upward-sloping saving curve, the new equilibrium has a higher real rate and more private investment. A higher rate alone does not prove crowding out when investment demand also changes.

before.q: Why is it misleading to multiply the entire actual federal debt by one market rate without qualification?
options: Federal debt never pays interest
One rate is only a simplifying assumption
Annual interest costs depend only on the current level of GDP
Every outstanding Treasury security carries the current market interest rate
before.feedback: A classroom uniform-rate calculation can illustrate the channel but does not describe the actual debt portfolio exactly.

after.q: In a simplified debt portfolio, $600 billion remains at a fixed 2 percent annual rate and $400 billion is refinanced from 2 to 5 percent at the start of the year. Principal stays constant; rates apply for the full year and there are no interest receipts. Revenues and noninterest outlays are unchanged. How do interest outlays and the deficit change?
options: Interest outlays become $50 billion and the deficit widens $30 billion
Interest outlays become $32 billion and the deficit widens $12 billion
Interest outlays become $20 billion and the deficit is unchanged
Interest outlays become $32 billion and the deficit widens $32 billion
after.feedback: Initial interest is (600 + 400)(0.02) = $20 billion. New interest is 600(0.02) + 400(0.05) = 12 + 20 = $32 billion. The $12 billion increase widens the deficit by the same amount. The current refinancing rate applies only to the repriced portion, not the whole portfolio.

reason: State financing assumptions and replace qualitative reconciliation with linked ratio and stock-growth reasoning.

before.q: Debt-to-GDP falls while the government runs a deficit. Which statement is most accurate?
options: A deficit always raises the ratio
A falling ratio proves the nominal debt stock also declined
Debt rises, but faster GDP growth lowers the ratio
GDP growth affects output but cannot affect a debt-to-GDP ratio
before.feedback: The deficit concerns the debt numerator's direction, while denominator growth can dominate the ratio.

after.q: A government begins with debt equal to 80 percent of nominal GDP. During the year it borrows an amount equal to 4 percent of initial GDP to finance its deficit, with no other debt adjustments. Nominal GDP grows 8 percent. Which result reconciles the deficit, the debt stock and the debt ratio?
options: Debt rises 4 percent, and debt-to-GDP falls to exactly 76 percent
Debt falls 4 percent, so debt-to-GDP falls to about 77.8 percent
Debt rises 5 percent, but debt-to-GDP falls to about 77.8 percent
Debt rises 5 percent, so debt-to-GDP rises to 84 percent
after.feedback: Normalize initial GDP to 100: debt starts at 80, borrowing adds 4 and GDP rises to 108. Debt growth is 4 / 80 = 5 percent; the new ratio is 84 / 108 ≈ 77.8 percent. Faster denominator growth lowers the ratio despite the borrowing-financed deficit.

reason: Replace one-step upper percentage-point arithmetic with denominator-aware reconstruction.

before.q: Debt-to-GDP increases from 80 percent to 88 percent. Which statement is correct?
options: The ratio rose 8 percent and 10 percentage points
The increase is 88 percentage points, or 8 percent of the initial ratio
The increase is 10 percentage points, or 8 percent of the initial ratio
The increase is 8 points, or 10 percent of the initial ratio
before.feedback: The level change is 8 points; dividing 8 by the initial 80 gives a 10 percent relative increase.

after.q: Debt-to-GDP rises from 80 percent to 88 percent while nominal GDP rises 5 percent. The debt measure and accounting dates are comparable. Which comparison correctly separates the ratio change from the change in nominal debt?
options: The ratio rises 8 percentage points, or 10 percent; nominal debt rises 10 percent
The ratio rises 8 percent, or 10 percentage points; nominal debt rises 13 percent
The ratio rises 8 percentage points, or 10 percent; nominal debt rises 5 percent
The ratio rises 8 percentage points, or 10 percent; nominal debt rises 15.5 percent
after.feedback: The ratio increases by 8 points and by 8 / 80 = 10 percent relative to its initial level. Nominal debt changes by the ratio factor times the GDP factor: (88 / 80)(1.05) = 1.155, or 15.5 percent. The ratio growth rate is not the numerator growth rate when GDP also changes.

before.q: CBO's February 2026 baseline projects debt held by the public at 101 percent of GDP in 2026 and 120 percent in 2036. Which conclusion is warranted?
options: The figures are realized nominal debt totals stated in trillions of dollars
GDP falls exactly 19 percent
Total public debt and debt held by the public are identical measures
The projected ratio rises from 101 to 120 percent
before.feedback: The comparison is a projected ratio for debt held by the public, not a realized nominal total.

after.q: CBO’s February 2026 baseline gives projected debt-held-by-the-public ratios of 101 percent of GDP in 2026 and 120 percent in 2036. Using only these displayed ratios, when would nominal debt in 2036 exceed nominal debt in 2026?
options: When nominal GDP in 2036 exceeds 120 percent of its 2026 level; a smaller GDP increase implies falling debt
Only when nominal GDP is unchanged; otherwise the two debt ratios cannot be compared
For every possible positive GDP level in 2036; a higher ratio proves a larger nominal debt stock
When nominal GDP in 2036 exceeds about 84.2 percent of its 2026 level; the ratios alone do not establish GDP’s change
after.feedback: Debt is its GDP share times nominal GDP. Thus 1.20 × GDP2036 must exceed 1.01 × GDP2026, requiring GDP2036 / GDP2026 > 101 / 120 ≈ 0.8417. A higher ratio alone does not identify nominal-debt growth without denominator evidence. This threshold uses the displayed rounded ratios and is not a forecast of GDP.

reason: Deepen the existing projected-ratio checkpoint through reverse consistency rather than a repeated subtraction.

before.q: CBO's February 2026 baseline projects debt held by the public at 101 percent of GDP in 2026 and 120 percent in 2036. What does the comparison imply?
options: An annual deficit increase of exactly 19 percent of GDP
A projected increase of 19 percentage points
A projected decline in debt held by the public measured in dollars
A projected GDP level equal to 120 percent of federal debt
before.feedback: The ratio rises from 101 to 120 percent, a 19-percentage-point increase in the projected debt stock relative to GDP.

after.q: CBO’s February 2026 baseline projects debt held by the public at 101 percent of GDP in 2026 and 120 percent in 2036. An analyst claims that nominal debt would therefore rise 19 percent. For that nominal-debt growth claim to be consistent with these displayed ratios, what would nominal GDP have to do?
options: Rise by 19 percent; debt and GDP must grow at the same rate when the ratio increases
Rise by about 0.16 percent; the 19-percentage-point ratio increase is not itself nominal-debt growth
Remain exactly unchanged; subtracting the two ratios gives the percent growth in debt
Fall by about 15.8 percent; a higher debt ratio necessarily implies a smaller economy
after.feedback: Let GDP growth have factor g. The nominal-debt factor would be (120 / 101)g. Setting it to 1.19 gives g = 1.19(101 / 120) ≈ 1.001583, a 0.16 percent increase. This is a conditional consistency calculation using displayed rounded ratios, not CBO’s GDP projection.
